l: Simon the Pharisee, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Simon is a Pharisee who hosts Jesus for a meal, doubting privately that Jesus is a prophet because he lets a sinful woman touch him. Jesus' parable of two debtors leads Simon to concede, then Jesus contrasts Simon's neglect with the woman's devotion.

l: sinful woman, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A woman known in the city as a sinner enters Simon's house, weeps at Jesus' feet, wipes, kisses and anoints them with ointment. Jesus declares her many sins forgiven because she loved much, says her faith saved her, and sends her in peace.

l: parable of the sower, The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_meaning the seed is the word of God [Jesus' explanation] Jesus tells of a farmer whose seed falls along the road, on rock, among thorns, and on good ground, where it yields a hundredfold. He explains that the seed is the word of God and the soils are different hearers: those from whom the devil takes the word, those who fall away in temptation, those choked by cares, riches and pleasures, and those who hold it tightly and bear fruit with perseverance.

l: storm (wind and water), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A wind storm comes down on the lake while Jesus sleeps in the boat, and the boat takes on dangerous amounts of water. Jesus rebukes the wind and the raging water, and they cease and it becomes calm, leaving the disciples asking who he is that even winds and water obey him.

l: possessed man (Legion), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A man from the city of the Gadarenes, long possessed by many demons, lived naked in the tombs and broke chains. He falls before Jesus, names himself Legion, and is freed. Found clothed and in his right mind at Jesus' feet, he is sent home instead of following, and proclaims throughout the city what Jesus did.

l: Jairus, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jairus is a synagogue ruler whose only daughter, about twelve, is dying. He begs Jesus to come; after news of her death, Jesus urges belief, and Jairus and his wife witness her being raised, told to tell no one.

l: Jairus' daughter, The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_age about twelve years Jairus' only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying and then dies before Jesus arrives. Jesus says she is sleeping, takes her by the hand and calls 'Child, arise!'; her spirit returns, she rises immediately, and he orders that she be given something to eat.

l: woman with flow of blood, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A woman suffering a flow of blood for twelve years, having spent everything on physicians without healing, touches the fringe of Jesus' cloak and is healed instantly. She confesses publicly, trembling; he calls her 'Daughter,' credits her faith, and sends her in peace.

l: multitude (at Bethsaida), The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_size about five thousand men The multitudes follow Jesus when he withdraws toward Bethsaida, and he welcomes them, speaks to them of God's Kingdom and cures those needing healing. About five thousand men are seated in groups of about fifty and all eat and are filled.

l: feeding of the five thousand, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Near Bethsaida in a desert region, Jesus has the twelve feed a crowd of about five thousand men from five loaves and two fish; he blesses and breaks them, all eat their fill, twelve baskets remain.

l: transfiguration, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The transfiguration is an event on a mountain where Jesus, praying with Peter, John and James, is changed in appearance; Moses and Elijah appear speaking of his departure, a cloud and a voice call him beloved Son, and the three stay silent.

l: boy (the man's son), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A man's only child, tormented by an unclean spirit causing cries, convulsions, foaming and bruising. The disciples fail to expel it; Jesus rebukes the spirit, heals the boy, and returns him to his father.

l: Jesus's suffering, death and resurrection, The Gospel According to Luke
s: involves_rejection_by elders, chief priests, and scribes [predicted] Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and be raised the third day. He later says he will be delivered into the hands of men, but the disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask. Moses and Elijah also speak of his departure to be accomplished at Jerusalem.

l: discipleship, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Discipleship is the topic of what following Jesus demands. Its conditions are self-denial, bearing one's own cross, renouncing all one has, and disregarding family and one's own life. In Chapter 9, Jesus tells followers to deny themselves, take up the cross, and lose their lives to save them, adding that the least is greatest, and answering three would-be followers: no place to lay one's head, no delay for burying a father, no looking back. In Chapter 14, he tells the multitudes these conditions are required, ending with the tasteless salt saying.

l: seventy others, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The seventy are laborers appointed by Jesus and sent two by two ahead of him as lambs among wolves to heal and proclaim God's Kingdom. They return joyful over demons' subjection, receive authority over the enemy, and are told to rejoice their names are written in heaven.

l: Hades, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Hades is a place of torment where the rich man, after death, suffers in flame, separated from Abraham's bosom and Lazarus by an uncrossable great gulf.

l: lawyer, The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_disposition desire to justify himself A lawyer stands up to test Jesus by asking what he must do to inherit eternal life. He correctly answers with the command to love God and neighbor, then, desiring to justify himself, asks who his neighbor is. After Jesus' parable he answers that the one who showed mercy was the neighbor, and is told to go and do likewise.

l: man attacked by robbers, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A man traveling from Jerusalem down to Jericho in Jesus' parable is stripped, beaten and left half dead by robbers; a priest and Levite pass by, but a Samaritan bandages him and pays for his care.

l: Samaritan, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The Samaritan is a character in a parable, defined by compassion. He sees a man attacked by robbers, bandages his wounds, carries him to an inn, pays the host two denarii and promises more, and is named the neighbor who showed mercy.

l: Martha, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Martha, Mary's sister, is an anxious, troubled woman who receives Jesus into her house, grows distracted with serving, asks him to make Mary help, and is told only one thing is needed.

l: disciples, The Gospel According to Luke
s: have_value_greater_than sparrows [hairs all counted] The disciples are addressed first, warned against the yeast of the Pharisees, told not to fear those who kill the body, and promised the Holy Spirit will teach them what to say before authorities. They are told not to be anxious about food or clothing, to seek God's Kingdom, to sell and give to the needy, and to be ready for the Son of Man's coming. Peter asks on their behalf whether the parable is for them or for everybody.

l: prayer, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray as John taught his disciples, and Jesus gives a prayer addressed to the Father asking for his name to be kept holy, his Kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from the evil one. He urges persistence in asking, seeking, and knocking, promising that everyone who asks receives.

l: friend at midnight (parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus tells of a man who goes to a friend at midnight to borrow three loaves for a visitor, and the friend inside refuses because the door is shut and his children are in bed. Jesus says that because of the man's persistence the friend will get up and give him as many as he needs.

l: demon (cast out by Jesus), The Gospel According to Luke
s: causes muteness [in the man it possessed] Jesus casts out a demon that made a man mute, and the man speaks, causing the crowds to marvel. The act prompts both the accusation of collusion with Beelzebul and the demand for a sign.

l: this generation, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus calls this generation evil for seeking a heavenly sign, promising only the sign of Jonah, then warns the Queen of the South and Nineveh's men will condemn it and the prophets' blood be required.

l: Jonah, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jonah is a prophet whose preaching led the Ninevites to repent; later he is cited as a sign to this generation, with one greater than Jonah present.

l: woes against Pharisees and lawyers, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus pronounces three woes on the Pharisees, for tithing herbs but neglecting justice and love, loving the best seats and greetings, and being like hidden graves. He pronounces three on the lawyers, for burdening people, building tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and taking away the key of knowledge. The woes provoke the anger of the scribes and Pharisees.

l: multitude, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_called hypocrites [fails to interpret this time] A multitude of many thousands gathers, so crowded that they trample on each other. One man from it asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide an inheritance with him and is answered with a warning against covetousness. Later Jesus calls the multitudes hypocrites for being able to read the earth and sky but not interpreting this time.

l: rich man (in the parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A rich man in the parable whose ground yields abundantly. He plans bigger barns to store his goods and then to relax, eat, drink, and be merry. God calls him foolish, requires his soul that night, and questions who gets his goods; he lays up treasure for himself, not rich toward God.

l: covetousness, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_warned_against_by Jesus (the speaker) [life is not abundance of possessions] Jesus tells the crowd to beware of and keep themselves from covetousness, because a man's life does not consist of the abundance of his possessions. The parable of the rich man who stores up goods illustrates its folly. It is contrasted with selling possessions, giving to the needy, and storing treasure in the heavens.

l: anxiety about necessities, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_forbidden_by Jesus (the speaker) [regarding food and clothing] Jesus tells his disciples not to be anxious about what they will eat or wear, since life is more than food and the body more than clothing. He notes that being anxious cannot add a cubit to one's height, and points to ravens and lilies as examples of God's provision. He says the nations seek these things but the Father knows the disciples need them, and that seeking God's Kingdom will bring them.

l: watchful servants, The Gospel According to Luke
s: are_served_by lord (in the watchfulness parable) [when found watching] Jesus tells his hearers to have their waists dressed and lamps burning, like men watching for their lord's return from a wedding feast. Those servants found watching are blessed, and the lord will dress himself, make them recline, and serve them, even if he comes in the second or third watch. The image is tied to being ready for the Son of Man, who comes in an unexpected hour.

l: faithful steward, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A faithful and wise steward, described by Jesus in answer to Peter, is set over his lord's household to give food portions at right times. If found so doing on the lord's return, he is blessed and set over all the lord has; an unfaithful servant is punished.

l: division in households, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_caused_by Jesus (the speaker) [he came to bring division rather than peace] Jesus says he has come to bring division on the earth rather than peace. He states that five in one house will be divided, three against two and two against three. He lists father against son, mother against daughter, and mother-in-law against daughter-in-law, with each pair also opposed in reverse.

l: fig tree parable, The Gospel According to Luke
s: features fig tree (the man's vineyard) [planted in the vineyard, bore no fruit for three years] A man whose fig tree in his vineyard has produced no fruit for three years tells the vine dresser to cut it down for wasting the soil. The vine dresser asks to leave it one more year while he digs around it and fertilizes it. If it bears fruit it stays; if not, it may be cut down.

l: woman with a spirit of infirmity, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A woman, called a daughter of Abraham, bent over eighteen years by a spirit of infirmity and bound by Satan, could not straighten up; Jesus called her, freed her, laid hands on her, and she stood straight, glorifying God.

l: ruler of the synagogue, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A synagogue ruler who holds that healing is not permitted on the Sabbath. Indignant at Jesus healing on that day, he told the crowd to seek healing on the six work days; Jesus called him and his companions hypocrites, and his adversaries were left disappointed.

l: narrow door, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_entered_by those who strive [many will seek to enter and be unable] In answer to whether few are saved, Jesus urges people to strive to enter by the narrow door, saying many will seek to enter and not be able. Once the master of the house has shut the door, those outside who knock and claim to have eaten and drunk in his presence will be told he does not know them and to depart, workers of iniquity.

l: repentance, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Repentance is a theme in Jesus' teaching, required to avoid perishing. In Chapter 13, after the Galileans killed by Pilate and the eighteen killed by the Siloam tower, he twice warns that unless hearers repent they will all perish, denying the victims were worse sinners; the fig tree parable offers another year. In Chapter 15, heaven rejoices over one repenting sinner, shown by the returning younger son's confession and welcome.

l: ruler of the Pharisees (host of the Sabbath meal), The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_a ruler of the Pharisees He hosts a Sabbath meal at his house where Jesus is watched. Jesus tells him not to invite friends, brothers, kinsmen, or rich neighbors who can repay him, but the poor, maimed, lame, and blind, and he will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.

l: man with dropsy, The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_condition dropsy A man with dropsy is in front of Jesus at the meal. Jesus takes him, heals him, and lets him go.

l: healing on the Sabbath, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus asks the lawyers and Pharisees whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful, and they do not answer. He heals the man with dropsy anyway and justifies it by the example of rescuing a son or ox from a well.

l: best seats and lowest place, The Gospel According to Luke
s: advised_choice lowest place [when invited to a wedding feast] Jesus notices that the invited guests choose the best seats. He teaches that at a wedding feast one should take the lowest place, so the host may say 'Friend, move up higher' and the guest be honored, rather than being shamed by being told to make room for someone more honorable.

l: humility and exaltation, The Gospel According to Luke
s: principle the self-exalted will be humbled; the self-humbled will be exalted Jesus states that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. This closes his teaching about seats at the wedding feast.

l: the poor, maimed, lame, and blind, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A group of people lacking resources to repay: the poor, maimed, lame, and blind. Jesus tells his Pharisee host to invite them to feasts for blessing, and in the parable the supper host brings them in after invited guests refuse.

l: man who made a great supper, The Gospel According to Luke
s: invites invited guests who made excuses [many people] In Jesus' parable, he invites many to a great supper and becomes angry when they make excuses. He orders his servant to bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame, then to compel people from the highways and hedges so his house is filled, and declares none of the invited men will taste his supper.

l: servant (of the supper host), The Gospel According to Luke
s: serves man who made a great supper [called lord and master of the house] The servant is sent at supper time to tell the invited that everything is ready, and reports their excuses to his lord. He brings in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame, reports there is still room, and is then sent to the highways and hedges to compel others to come in.

l: great supper, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The great supper is made by a man who invites many, and everything is ready at supper time. The invited refuse, so the house is filled with others, and the host says none of the originally invited will taste it.

l: invited guests who made excuses, The Gospel According to Luke
s: will_not_taste great supper [declared by the host] All the invited guests, as one, begin to make excuses: one has bought a field, one has bought five yoke of oxen, and one has married a wife. The host declares that none of them will taste his supper.

l: counting the cost, The Gospel According to Luke
s: illustrated_by tower building and a king weighing war [parables of discipleship] Jesus illustrates it with a man who wants to build a tower and sits down first to see if he can finish, lest he be mocked. He also cites a king who weighs ten thousand against twenty thousand and sends an envoy to ask for peace terms.

l: shepherd (man with one hundred sheep), The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_flock_size one hundred sheep [in the parable] In the parable, the man who loses one of his hundred sheep leaves the ninety-nine in the wilderness and goes after the lost one until he finds it. He carries it home on his shoulders rejoicing and calls his friends and neighbors to rejoice with him.

l: lost sheep (shepherd's sheep), The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_owned_by shepherd (man with one hundred sheep) The one sheep out of one hundred is lost and is sought until found. The shepherd carries it on his shoulders, and its finding is the occasion for rejoicing.

l: woman (with ten drachma coins), The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_coin_count ten [drachma coins] The woman who loses one of her ten drachma coins lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and seeks diligently until she finds it. She then calls her friends and neighbors to rejoice with her.

l: lost drachma coin (woman's coin), The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_owned_by woman (with ten drachma coins) One of the woman's ten drachma coins is lost and is found after she lights a lamp, sweeps, and searches. Its finding prompts her to call others to rejoice, and Jesus compares this to the joy of the angels of God over one repenting sinner.

l: father (of the two sons), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A father of two sons divides his livelihood when the younger asks for his share. On the younger son's return he runs to him with compassion, embraces him, clothes him richly, and orders a feast. He then pleads with the angry elder son, affirming all is his and celebrating the lost-and-found brother.

l: younger son (prodigal), The Gospel According to Luke
s: The younger son, brother of the elder son, asks for his property share, wastes it on riotous living in a far country, and is reduced to feeding pigs in famine. He comes to himself, returns and confesses, and his father restores him as dead now alive, lost now found.

l: elder son, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The elder son is the obedient heir of all his father's possessions, who claims he never disobeyed a commandment. Hearing celebration for his returned brother, he grows angry, refuses to enter, and complains he never got even a goat. His father replies that he is always with him and all is his.

l: celebration (feast for the returned son), The Gospel According to Luke
s: The father orders a celebration with the fattened calf, best robe, ring and sandals for the returned younger son, and they begin to celebrate with music and dancing. The elder son's anger at it prompts the father to explain that it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad because the brother was dead and is alive, lost and found.

l: rich man (manager's lord), The Gospel According to Luke
s: The rich man learns his manager is wasting his possessions and demands an accounting, removing him from management. He later commends the dishonest manager for having acted wisely after the manager reduces the debtors' bills.

l: manager (dishonest manager), The Gospel According to Luke
s: The manager is accused of wasting his lord's possessions and told he will lose his position. Unable to dig and ashamed to beg, he has debtors cut their bills (oil from a hundred to fifty batos, wheat from a hundred to eighty cors) so they will receive him into their houses, and his lord commends his wisdom.

l: mammon, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_characterized_as unrighteous Mammon is called unrighteous, and Jesus urges making friends by means of it so that others may receive the disciples into the eternal tents. He says no one can serve both God and Mammon.

l: rich man (in Lazarus parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A rich man in a parable who wears purple and fine linen and lives luxuriously while a beggar lies at his gate; after death he suffers in Hades, and his pleas to Abraham for relief and for warning his five brothers are refused.

l: Lazarus, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Lazarus, a sore-covered beggar at a rich man's gate, longs for crumbs while dogs lick his sores; after he dies, angels carry him to Abraham's bosom, comforted.

l: five brothers (rich man's brothers), The Gospel According to Luke
s: The rich man's five brothers are still living in his father's house, and he asks that Lazarus be sent to testify to them so they avoid the place of torment. Abraham answers that they have Moses and the prophets to listen to.

l: Samaritan leper (one of the ten lepers), The Gospel According to Luke
s: The Samaritan was cleansed with the other nine as they went to show themselves to the priests. He alone turned back, glorifying God loudly and falling at Jesus' feet in thanks, and Jesus told him to get up and go, saying his faith had healed him.

l: ten lepers, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Ten men with leprosy beg Jesus for mercy, are told to show themselves to the priests, and all are cleansed en route; only one returns to give thanks, prompting Jesus to ask about the nine.

l: forgiveness, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_required_when brother repents [even seven times a day] Jesus instructs that if a brother sins, he should be rebuked, and if he repents, he must be forgiven. This applies even if he sins seven times in a day and seven times returns saying 'I repent.'

l: faith, The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_power_like mustard seed [even a grain-sized faith could uproot a sycamore tree] When the apostles ask for increased faith, Jesus says faith like a mustard seed could make a sycamore tree uproot and plant itself in the sea. He later tells the thankful Samaritan that his faith has healed him.

l: coming of the Son of Man, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The coming of the Son of Man is described as sudden and unmistakable, like lightning flashing across the sky. It must first be preceded by his suffering and rejection by this generation. Likened to the days of Noah and Lot, ordinary life ends in sudden destruction, one taken, another left.

l: unrighteous judge (parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A city judge who neither fears God nor respects people; he first refuses a widow's plea, then, worn down by her persistent coming, decides to defend her.

l: widow (parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A widow in the judge's city, opposed by an adversary, repeatedly comes to the judge seeking defense; her persistence ultimately wins her the defense she wanted.

l: Son of Man, The Gospel According to Luke
s: will_come_in a cloud [with power and great glory] Jesus says people will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. He tells his listeners to pray to be counted worthy to stand before the Son of Man.

l: Pharisee (parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A Pharisee in a parable who prays in the temple, thanking God he is unlike others or the tax collector, citing fasting and tithing; Jesus declares the tax collector justified instead, since self-exalters will be humbled.

l: tax collector (parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A tax collector goes up to the temple to pray, stands far off, beats his chest, and begs God's mercy as a sinner; Jesus says he went home justified, unlike the Pharisee.

l: babies and little children, The Gospel According to Luke
s: belongs_to God's Kingdom [Kingdom belongs to such as these] People bring babies to Jesus to be touched, and the disciples rebuke them. Jesus summons them, tells the disciples not to hinder them, and says God's Kingdom belongs to such as these and must be received like a little child.

l: rich ruler, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A very rich ruler, observant of the commandments since youth, asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life; told to sell everything and follow him, he grows very sad.

l: blind man, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A blind beggar by the road near Jericho hears Jesus passing, persistently cries out for mercy despite rebuke, receives sight through faith, then follows Jesus glorifying God.

l: prayer, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus teaches that people must always pray and not give up, illustrated by the persistent widow. The Pharisee's self-righteous prayer contrasts with the tax collector's humble plea for mercy, which Jesus says leads to justification.

l: Zacchaeus, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Zacchaeus is a rich, short chief tax collector, labeled a sinner by the murmuring crowd. He climbs a sycamore to see Jesus, welcomes him joyfully, pledges half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution, and Jesus declares salvation has come to his house.

l: parable of the minas, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A parable told by Jesus near Jerusalem to correct the belief that God's Kingdom would appear immediately: a nobleman leaves to receive a kingdom, rewards servants by gains, takes the hidden mina, and has enemies killed.

l: nobleman (in the parable), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A nobleman in a parable, called exacting by his third servant, who travels to a far country to receive a kingdom. He entrusts ten servants with ten minas, is hated by citizens who send an envoy opposing him, then returns, rewards the faithful servants with cities, judges the third by his words, and orders enemies killed.

l: servants (of the nobleman), The Gospel According to Luke
s: Ten servants are each given a mina and told to conduct business until the nobleman comes; two who earned ten and five minas gain authority over cities, while one who hid his out of fear is called wicked and loses it.

l: colt, The Gospel According to Luke
s: An unridden colt, owned by others, is found tied in the village as Jesus foretold; disciples say the Lord needs it, bring it to him, cover it with cloaks, and seat him on it.

l: destruction of Jerusalem (Jesus' prophecy), The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_a foretold desolation [predicted by Jesus] Jesus predicts that when Jerusalem is surrounded by armies its desolation is near, and he tells those in Judea to flee to the mountains. He calls these days of vengeance fulfilling what is written, with great distress, wrath on the people, death by the sword, and captivity among the nations.

l: priests and scribes, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Priests and scribes, with elders, oppose Jesus: they challenge his authority, cannot answer about John's baptism for fear of the people, seek to seize him, send spies, and are warned of greater condemnation for craving honor and devouring widows' houses.

l: authority of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The priests, scribes and elders ask by what authority Jesus does these things and who gave it to him. Jesus answers with a counter-question and then declines to tell them, since they would not answer his.

l: vineyard parable, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Parable told by Jesus to the people: farmers renting a vineyard beat three servants and kill the owner's son; the owner destroys them and gives the vineyard to others, and priests and scribes realize it targets them.

l: man (owner of the vineyard), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A vineyard owner in a parable plants a vineyard, rents it to farmers, and goes abroad. He sends three servants, then his beloved son, for his share, and will destroy the farmers and give the vineyard to others.

l: farmers, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Parable farmers tenant the owner's vineyard, beat and shame his servants, send them away empty or wounded, then kill the heir for the inheritance, and are told they will be destroyed and the vineyard given to others.

l: son (beloved son of the vineyard owner), The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_a heir [as the farmers recognized] The owner sends his beloved son in hope that the farmers will respect him. The farmers recognize him as the heir, throw him out of the vineyard and kill him.

l: Caesar, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Caesar's image and inscription are on the denarius that Jesus has the spies show him. Jesus says to give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

l: taxes to Caesar, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The spies flatter Jesus and ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, hoping to trap him before the governor. He has them name Caesar's image on a denarius and tells them to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, and they are silenced.

l: Sadducees, The Gospel According to Luke
s: deny resurrection The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask Jesus about a woman who married seven brothers in turn and whose wife she will be in the resurrection. Jesus answers that the resurrected neither marry nor die and that God is God of the living.

l: resurrection, The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_property neither marry nor are given in marriage [for those worthy to attain it] Jesus says those considered worthy of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage and cannot die any more, being like the angels and children of God. He cites Moses at the bush as showing that the dead are raised.

l: poor widow, The Gospel According to Luke
s: gave all she had to live on [out of her poverty] A poor widow casts two small brass coins into the treasury. Jesus says she put in more than all the rich givers, because they gave from their abundance while she gave all she had to live on.

l: disciples (Jesus' listeners), The Gospel According to Luke
s: promised not a hair of their heads will perish Some of Jesus' listeners talk about the temple's decoration, then ask when the destruction will come and what the sign will be. Jesus warns them not to be led astray or terrified, tells them not to prepare their defense beforehand, promises not a hair of their heads will perish, and urges endurance and watchfulness.

l: persecution of followers, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus foretells that before other events his followers will be seized, persecuted, imprisoned and brought before rulers for his name's sake, betrayed by family and friends, some killed, all hated. This becomes a testimony; he gives them unanswerable wisdom, and endurance wins their lives.

l: signs in the heavens and on earth, The Gospel According to Luke
s: include signs in the sun, moon, and stars Jesus describes wars, nations rising against nations, great earthquakes, famines, plagues, terrors, and great signs from heaven. He adds signs in the sun, moon, and stars, anxiety among nations over the roaring sea, and people fainting for fear as the powers of the heavens are shaken. He says that when these begin, his followers should lift their heads because their redemption is near, and that they signal God's Kingdom is near, like budding fig trees signal summer.

l: chief priests, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The chief priests, with scribes and elders, are a group set on putting Jesus to death while fearing the people. They agree to pay Judas, come against Jesus with swords and clubs, and convene a council that declares no more witness is needed after he claims to be Son of God. They then accuse him before Herod and Pilate, secure his crucifixion, and scoff at him.

l: Last Supper, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A Passover meal in a large, furnished upper room with the twelve apostles. Jesus shares a cup, gives bread as his body and the cup as the new covenant in his blood, announces a betrayer, hears a dispute over greatness, and warns Peter of denial.

l: prayer in Gethsemane, The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_location Mount of Olives On the Mount of Olives Jesus tells the disciples to pray not to enter temptation, withdraws about a stone's throw, kneels, and asks the Father to remove the cup while submitting to his will. An angel from heaven strengthens him, and in agony his sweat becomes like great drops of blood. He returns to find the disciples sleeping from grief and tells them to rise and pray.

l: arrest of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus's arrest is led by Judas, who arrives with a crowd and approaches to kiss him. A disciple cuts off the high priest's servant's ear; Jesus heals it, calls this their hour of darkness's power, is seized, and taken to the high priest's house, mocked and beaten.

l: Peter's denial, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_a fulfilled prediction [Jesus foretold three denials before the rooster crowed] In the courtyard of the high priest's house, a servant girl, then another person, then a third after about an hour say Peter was with Jesus. Peter denies it each time, saying he does not know him, is not one of them, and does not know what they mean. A rooster crows immediately after the third denial, Jesus looks at him, Peter remembers the prediction, and he goes out and weeps bitterly.

l: Barabbas, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_imprisoned_for revolt and murder [thrown into prison] Barabbas is described as a prisoner thrown into prison for a revolt in the city and for murder. The crowd demands his release instead of Jesus, and Pilate releases him.

l: criminal (repentant), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A repentant criminal crucified beside Jesus, condemned alongside him, believes Jesus innocent, rebukes the other criminal's insults, asks to be remembered in the Kingdom, and is promised Paradise that day.

l: Joseph of Arimathaea, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Joseph of Arimathaea is a good, righteous council member awaiting God's Kingdom who did not consent to the council's deed; he asks Pilate for Jesus' body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in an unused tomb.

l: The Skull, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_site_of crucifixion of Jesus The Skull is the place where Jesus is led and crucified with two criminals, one on his right and one on his left.

l: tomb, The Gospel According to Luke
s: A stone-cut tomb, never used before, where Joseph lays Jesus' wrapped body on Preparation day while the Galilean women watch how it is placed.

l: Jesus' crucifixion and suffering, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus is crucified at The Skull between two criminals, with soldiers dividing his garments by lot and an inscription reading 'THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.' He is mocked by rulers, soldiers, and one criminal; from the sixth to ninth hour darkness covers the land, the temple veil tears, and he dies. The centurion glorifies God, and the crowds return home beating their chests.

l: trial of Jesus, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus is tried before Pilate, sent to Herod, and returned, with Pilate finding no basis for a charge. The crowd and chief priests demand crucifixion and the release of Barabbas, and Pilate decrees that their request be done.

l: women (Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James), The Gospel According to Luke
s: A group of women including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James find the tomb empty, hear from two men that Jesus is risen, and tell the apostles, who dismiss it as nonsense.

l: tomb (Jesus' tomb), The Gospel According to Luke
s: has_state empty [Jesus' body not found] The tomb is found with its stone rolled away and Jesus' body not inside. Peter later runs there, stoops, and sees only the strips of linen lying by themselves; other disciples also go and find it as the women said.

l: two men (angels at the tomb), The Gospel According to Luke
s: wears dazzling clothing Two men in dazzling clothing stand by the women at the tomb and terrify them. They ask why the women seek the living among the dead, announce that Jesus is risen, and remind them of what he said in Galilee about being delivered up, crucified, and rising on the third day. The Emmaus disciples later describe them as a vision of angels who said he was alive.

l: Cleopas, The Gospel According to Luke
s: is_member_of two disciples (on the road to Emmaus) Cleopas is one of two disciples walking to Emmaus. He answers the unrecognized Jesus by asking if he is the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn't know what has happened, and he recounts Jesus' death, their lost hope of redemption, and the women's report of the empty tomb.

l: two disciples (on the road to Emmaus), The Gospel According to Luke
s: travels_to Emmaus [on the day of the resurrection] Two disciples walk to Emmaus that day, talking about the events, and their eyes are kept from recognizing Jesus when he joins them. They urge him to stay, recognize him at the breaking of the bread, and say their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures. They return at once to Jerusalem and tell the eleven what happened on the way.

l: Emmaus, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Emmaus is a village sixty stadia from Jerusalem; two disciples travel there on resurrection day, Jesus stays with them, and they recognize him at table before he vanishes.

l: Scriptures, The Gospel According to Luke
s: concerns Jesus [Moses, the prophets and the psalms] Jesus explains to the Emmaus disciples, beginning from Moses and all the prophets, the things concerning himself, and says the Christ had to suffer and enter his glory. He later says all that is written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms about him must be fulfilled, and he opens the disciples' minds to understand them.

l: breaking of the bread (meal at Emmaus), The Gospel According to Luke
s: At the table in Emmaus, Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to the two disciples. Their eyes are opened and they recognize him, and then he vanishes. They later relate that he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.

l: Jesus' resurrection, The Gospel According to Luke
s: The two men announce that Jesus is risen, and the report is confirmed when Jesus appears to Simon, to the Emmaus disciples, and to the gathered group. He shows his hands and feet, says a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones, and eats in front of them. He says it was written that the Christ would suffer and rise from the dead the third day.

l: Jesus' ascension, The Gospel According to Luke
s: Jesus' ascension: at Bethany, after blessing the disciples with lifted hands, he withdraws and is carried up into heaven; they worship him and joyfully return to Jerusalem.

l: disciples (the eleven and companions in Jerusalem), The Gospel According to Luke
s: The eleven and their companions in Jerusalem first doubt the women's report, then say the Lord is risen. Terrified when Jesus appears, they are convinced by his hands, feet and eating. He names them witnesses of his resurrection and tells them to wait for power; after his ascension they worship and continually praise God in the temple.

l: The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Acts of the Apostles is a narrative, addressed to Theophilus, of how the message about Jesus spreads from Jerusalem to Rome after his ascension. Its central figures are Peter, who leads the early chapters, and Paul (earlier Saul), who dominates the second half, with Barnabas, Philip, Stephen, James, Silas, and Timothy playing important supporting roles. After forty days of appearances, Jesus promises the apostles the Holy Spirit and power to be witnesses to the ends of the earth, then ascends. Matthias replaces Judas. At Pentecost the believers are filled with the Spirit and speak in many languages; Peter preaches and about three thousand join. The community shares goods, Peter and John heal a lame man, and the apostles face arrest, threats, and a beating from the council but keep teaching. Ananias and Sapphira die for deceit. Seven men, including Stephen, are chosen to serve; Stephen's speech before the council ends with his stoning while Saul looks on. Persecution scatters believers. Philip preaches in Samaria and baptizes an Ethiopian eunuch. Saul, on the road to Damascus, meets Jesus, is blinded, healed by Ananias, baptized, and begins preaching; Barnabas brings him to the apostles. Peter, after a vision, preaches to Cornelius's Gentile household, who receive the Spirit, and defends this in Jerusalem. Antioch becomes a centre where disciples are first called Christians. Herod kills James and jails Peter, who is freed by an angel; Herod is struck down. Barnabas and Saul, now called Paul, are sent out from Antioch, preaching in Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, turning to the Gentiles amid opposition and stoning. A Jerusalem council, hearing Peter and James, decides Gentiles need not be circumcised. Paul and Barnabas part; Paul takes Silas, then Timothy, through Macedonia and Greece: Philippi (Lydia, the jailer), Thessalonica, Beroea, Athens (the Areopagus), Corinth, and Ephesus, where he teaches two years and a riot erupts over Artemis. He gives a farewell to Ephesian elders at Miletus. In Jerusalem Paul is seized in the temple, defends himself before the crowd and council, and, after a plot to kill him, is sent to Felix at Caesarea. He is held two years, then, under Festus, appeals to Caesar and speaks before Agrippa, who finds nothing deserving death. Sailing to Rome, he survives a storm and shipwreck and a viper bite on Malta. In Rome he testifies to Jewish leaders, declares salvation sent to the nations, and spends two years preaching boldly without hindrance.

l: Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Jesus is the central figure of these records: a man from Nazareth, son of Mary with brothers, and Son of God whose Father is God. He was approved by God through mighty works, wonders and signs, and anointed with the Holy Spirit and power. He went about doing good and healing those oppressed by the devil. He is called Servant of God, Holy and Righteous One, Prince of life, Prince and Savior, Christ, and Lord of all. The records open with him chosen apostles, giving them commandment through the Holy Spirit, and showing himself alive to them by many proofs over forty days after he suffered. He told them to wait for the Father's promise, said they would be witnesses, and was taken up in a cloud, with a promise that he would return the same way. The early chapters recount that lawless men, the Jerusalem people and rulers, crucified or killed him by hanging on a tree, by God's determined counsel, though no cause for death was found. God raised him from the dead without decay, exalted him to his right hand, and made him Lord and Christ. Heaven receives him until the times of restoration of all things. He is the rejected stone that became the head of the corner, and there is no other name under heaven by which people must be saved. Faith in his name heals the lame man, and the apostles keep preaching and teaching him despite the council's command and suffering. Stephen sees him standing at God's right hand and calls on him as Lord. He is appointed Judge of the living and the dead, and everyone who believes in his name receives forgiveness of sins. The story then spreads outward: Philip preaches to the Samaritans and the eunuch, Gentiles receive the same gift, and believers preach the Lord Jesus in Antioch. Jesus himself speaks to Saul from a light, identifies himself as the one Saul persecuted, and appoints him servant and witness to Jews and Gentiles, to bear his name before nations and kings. Paul then proclaims in synagogues and cities that Jesus is the Christ who had to suffer and rise, a Saviour from David's offspring, and that God will judge the world by him. The records end in Rome with Paul teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness.

l: Holy Spirit, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Holy Spirit appears in these records as a divine agent who speaks, directs, empowers and is given, rather than a mere force. Promised by Jesus in Chapter 1 as a baptism that would bring power to the apostles, he is also said to have spoken through David about Judas. In Chapter 2 he fills the gathered believers, who speak in other languages, and Peter teaches that Jesus received the promise from the Father and poured it out; repentant, baptized people will receive the gift. The Spirit then extends outward: Samaritan believers receive him through Peter and John's prayer and laying on of hands, Simon tries to buy this power, and the Spirit directs Philip to the eunuch and carries him away. In Chapters 10 and 11 he sends men to Peter and falls on Gentiles in Cornelius's house, amazing the circumcised believers. He fills Barnabas, informs Agabus of a famine, and in Chapter 13 directs the Antioch assembly to send out Barnabas and Saul, filling Paul against Elymas and the disciples with joy. In Chapter 19 Ephesian disciples, unfamiliar with him, receive him through Paul's hands, speak in languages and prophesy; Paul resolves in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem and Rome.

l: apostles, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The apostles are the group Jesus chose, told to wait in Jerusalem and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the farthest parts of the earth. After seeing him taken up, they return to Jerusalem, stay in the upper room, and pray with one accord alongside the women and Jesus' family. Their number is restored to twelve when Matthias is counted with the eleven after Judas fell away. They then testify to the resurrection with great power, perform signs and wonders, gather in Solomon's porch, and receive proceeds that believers lay at their feet for distribution according to need. Jailed by the high priest and freed by an angel, they keep teaching in the temple and at home despite being beaten and commanded to stop, leaving rejoicing. Finally, to avoid forsaking the word of God to serve tables, they have disciples select seven men to oversee daily service, pray and lay hands on them, and themselves continue in prayer and the ministry of the word.

l: God, The Acts of the Apostles
s: God is portrayed throughout these records as the living God, creator of the sky, earth, sea and all in them, and Lord of heaven and earth, who does not dwell in temples made with hands. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who made a covenant and promise with the fathers, gave the covenant of circumcision to Abraham, chose Israel and exalted the people, and gave David as king, a man after his heart. He appears to Abraham and Moses, is with Joseph in Egypt, and led the fathers out of Egypt. The most important thread is what he does with Jesus. He approved Jesus by wonders, anointed him with the Holy Spirit and power, and raised him from the dead, freeing him from the agony of death. He exalted him to his right hand as Prince and Savior, made him Lord and Christ, and appointed him Judge of the living and the dead. He swore an oath to David to raise up the Christ, announced through the prophets that Christ would suffer, and will send Christ Jesus again. The resurrection is also called assurance of the coming day of judgment, when he will judge the world in righteousness. The account unfolds from the early preaching in Jerusalem, where he pours out his Spirit as promised, answers the believers' prayer by shaking the place and filling them with the Holy Spirit, and is said to be one who cannot be overthrown. In Samaria his Kingdom is preached and his gift cannot be bought. Then he widens his reach: he sends an angel to Cornelius, shows Peter through a vision not to call unclean what he has cleansed, shows no favoritism, accepts anyone in every nation who fears him and works righteousness, gives the Holy Spirit to the Gentiles as to the apostles, cleanses their hearts by faith, and opens a door of faith to the nations. He had allowed nations to walk their own ways, yet left witness through rains and fruitful seasons, and now commands all to repent. He takes a people for his name and purchased his flock with his own blood. At the end Paul declares that God raises the dead, that the promise to the fathers is hoped for by the twelve tribes, and that God's help sustains him.

l: John, The Acts of the Apostles
s: John, a member of the apostles, goes up to the temple with Peter, where a healed lame man clings to them as crowds gather at Solomon's porch. He is then arrested with Peter while speaking and held overnight; a different John appears at the council.

l: Jerusalem, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Jerusalem is a city that serves as the central place of the apostles' witness and authority throughout Acts. It is near Olivet, a Sabbath day's journey away, and its residents call Judas's field Akeldama, the field of blood. At the start, Jesus commands the apostles to wait there for the Father's promise, and they gather in the upper room. Persecution then arises there, scattering others while the apostles remain; they send Peter and John to Samaria, and Philip is sent along the road down to Gaza. Saul, who had made havoc of believers there, is feared after his conversion until Barnabas brings him to the apostles, and the Hellenists then seek to kill him. Jerusalem hosts the council where apostles and elders debate the circumcision question and send out a decision and letter. Later it becomes the dangerous destination for Paul: he is warned not to go, is received by James and the elders, and is accused in the temple, seized by a stirred-up crowd, and held in the barracks. Agabus's prophecy begins to be fulfilled. Finally, Jewish leaders there plot against Paul through Festus, and Paul refuses to be judged there.

l: Samaria, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Samaria received Philip's preaching of Christ, and there was great joy in the city. The apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God and sent Peter and John there.

l: Israel, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul's sermon recounts Israel's history: chosen fathers, deliverance from Egypt, forty years in the wilderness, the conquest of Canaan, judges, and the kings Saul and David. God brought salvation to Israel from David's offspring according to his promise, preceded by John's baptism of repentance to Israel.

l: Peter, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Peter, also called Simon, is an apostle and a Jew, listed first among the eleven, who believes in Jesus Christ as Lord and bears witness to his resurrection, often alongside John. He is a man, not to be worshiped, who has no silver or gold and has never eaten anything common or unclean. The records show him as a leading voice of the early believers, chosen by God so the nations would hear the Good News through his mouth. The account begins in the upper room, where Peter stands among about one hundred twenty disciples and says Scripture about Judas must be fulfilled and a witness to the resurrection chosen. In Chapter 2 he stands with the eleven, answers the mockers by pointing to Joel's prophecy, preaches Jesus' death and resurrection, and calls the crowd to repent and be baptized. In Chapter 3 he and John heal a lame man at the temple in Jesus' name, and Peter calls the astonished crowd to repent. In Chapter 4, filled with the Holy Spirit, he tells the rulers that salvation is in no other name. In Chapter 5 he confronts Ananias and Sapphira, who each die after his words; the sick are laid in the streets so his shadow might fall on them; and before the council he says they must obey God rather than men. In Chapter 8 the apostles send him with John from Jerusalem to Samaria, where they lay hands on believers to receive the Holy Spirit, and he rebukes Simon for trying to buy God's gift. In Chapter 9 he heals Aeneas at Lydda, raises Tabitha at Joppa, and stays many days with Simon the tanner. In Chapter 10, after the sheet vision, he goes with Cornelius's men to Caesarea, declares no man is unholy or unclean, and commands that the Gentile hearers be baptized after the Spirit falls on them. In Chapter 11 he defends this in Jerusalem and silences his critics. In Chapter 12 Herod seizes him and holds him under guard, bound by two chains. The church prays constantly, an angel of the Lord delivers him, and he tells the believers, asking them to inform James and the brothers, then departs. In Chapter 15 at the Jerusalem gathering he says God gave the Gentiles the Holy Spirit as to the Jewish believers, calls the law an unbearable yoke, and affirms that all are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus.

l: James, The Acts of the Apostles
s: gives_judgment not troubling Gentiles who turn to God [at the Jerusalem council] James speaks after Peter, citing Simeon's report and the words of the prophets about rebuilding David's tabernacle so the Gentiles may seek the Lord. He gives his judgment that Gentile turners to God not be troubled, but be told to abstain from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood.

l: Philip, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Philip is an evangelist and one of the seven. He goes down to Samaria, preaching Christ and performing signs and miracles, then, guided by an angel and the Spirit, explains Isaiah to an Ethiopian eunuch and baptizes him. Caught away by the Spirit, he appears at Azotus, preaches onward to Caesarea, and has four virgin daughters.

l: the Way (disciples of the Lord), The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Way is the community of the Lord's disciples, numbering about one hundred twenty and centered in Jerusalem. It grows steadily: the multitude chooses seven men, and many priests obey the faith. Saul first persecutes followers, then is received after conversion, while assemblies across Judea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoy peace and multiply. In Antioch they are first called Christians, and they send relief to Judean brothers.

l: David, The Acts of the Apostles
s: David, son of Jesse, was a prophet and patriarch who authored Psalms through the Holy Spirit. God raised him as king after Saul, a man after his heart. He died, saw decay, and his tomb remains in Jerusalem, while salvation came through his offspring, Jesus.

l: Judas, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Judas guided those who took Jesus, despite being counted among the apostles and sharing their ministry. He obtained a field Akeldama with the reward of his wickedness, fell headlong and burst open, and fell away to his own place, so the apostles prayed for another to take his place.

l: Matthias, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Matthias was a man nominated with Joseph Barsabbas to replace Judas; the lot fell on him, so he was chosen and counted with the eleven apostles.

l: Ascension of Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Jesus was taken up while the apostles watched, and a cloud received him out of sight. Two men in white told the Galileans he would return in the same way. The apostles then went back to Jerusalem from Olivet.

l: God's Kingdom, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_topic_of Jesus [spoken about during forty days] Paul explains and testifies about God's Kingdom to the many who come to his lodging in Rome. The chapter ends with him preaching it for two years with all boldness and without hindrance.

l: selection of Judas's replacement, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Peter says Judas's place must be filled by a man who accompanied them from John's baptism to the ascension, as a witness of the resurrection. Two candidates, Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias, are put forward; after prayer they draw lots, and the lot falls on Matthias, who is counted with the eleven.

l: disciples (believers gathered at Pentecost), The Acts of the Apostles
s: The disciples are the believers gathered as an assembly in Jerusalem. At Pentecost they are united, filled with the Holy Spirit, and speak in other languages; mockers call them drunk, yet about three thousand are baptized and join them. After Stephen's burial, great persecution under Saul scatters them across Judea and Samaria, and they preach wherever they go. Later Herod oppresses them, killing James and arresting Peter, while the assembly prays constantly and is amazed when Peter arrives freed.

l: multitude (Jews in Jerusalem), The Acts of the Apostles
s: includes devout Jews from every nation Devout Jews from every nation under the sky gather, bewildered and amazed to hear the believers speaking in their own native languages about the mighty works of God. Some are perplexed and others mock; after Peter's sermon they are cut to the heart and ask what to do, and about three thousand receive his word and are baptized.

l: Pentecost, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a day [the day the disciples were together] Pentecost is the day on which the believers are gathered in one place when the sound like a mighty wind comes and the Holy Spirit is poured out. It is also the day on which about three thousand souls are added to the believers.

l: speaking in other languages, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_enabled_by Holy Spirit Upon being filled with the Spirit, the believers speak in other languages, and people from many nations each hear them in their own native language declaring God's mighty works. The phenomenon causes amazement and perplexity in some and mockery in others, and Peter explains it as the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy.

l: Egypt, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Egypt is where Joseph is made governor and where famine brings Jacob's family for grain. Jacob and the fathers die there, and the people multiply until a king who did not know Joseph oppresses them. Moses grows up there and later leads the people out through wonders and signs, though the fathers' hearts turn back to it.

l: Rome, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Rome is where Paul arrives as a prisoner, delivered by the centurion to the captain of the guard. Brothers come out to meet him as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns, and in the city he meets the Jewish leaders and lives two years in a rented house.

l: Peter's Pentecost sermon, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_delivered_by Peter Peter addresses the men of Judea and Israel, declaring that the believers are not drunk but fulfilling Joel's prophecy, and that Jesus, crucified by lawless men, was raised by God as David foretold. He concludes that God has made this Jesus both Lord and Christ, which cuts the hearers to the heart.

l: resurrection of Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The resurrection of Jesus is God raising him from the dead, attested by disciples who accompanied him from Galilee to Jerusalem. Peter argues death could not hold him, citing David's foretelling. Paul later repeats that Jesus was seen many days, fulfilling the fathers' promise, and saw no decay unlike David.

l: baptism and repentance, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Baptism and repentance is the teaching that, when asked what to do, Peter urges everyone to repent and be baptized in Jesus Christ's name for forgiveness of sins, leading to the Holy Spirit's gift; about three thousand gladly received it and were baptized.

l: early church community life, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Early church community life: new believers steadfastly follow the apostles' teaching, fellowship, bread-breaking and prayer, amid awe and wonders. They share all things, sell possessions to meet needs, meet daily with gladness and praise, gain favor with all, and the Lord adds those being saved.

l: temple, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Stephen says David asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob, but Solomon built the house. He declares that the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, citing the prophet's words that heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool. Paul enters the temple to carry out the purification, and the Jews from Asia see him there. He is accused of defiling the holy place by bringing Greeks in, and the crowd drags him out and the doors are shut immediately.

l: lame man (healed by Peter and John), The Acts of the Apostles
s: A man over forty, lame from birth, is carried daily to the temple's Beautiful gate to beg. Peter raises him in Jesus' name; his feet gain strength and he enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, recognized by the people. He later stands whole before the council, and the rulers cannot speak against it.

l: temple, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_part Beautiful Gate (of the temple) [door called Beautiful] The temple is the place Peter and John go to at the hour of prayer, with its door called Beautiful where the lame man begs daily. The healed man enters it walking and praising God, and the people gather in Solomon's porch.

l: people (in the temple), The Acts of the Apostles
s: The men of Israel are the temple crowd, heirs of God's covenant with the fathers. They see the healed beggar walking and praising God, are amazed, and run to Peter and John, who rebuke them for denying Jesus in ignorance.

l: Abraham, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Abraham is a man called by God in Mesopotamia to leave his land, living in Haran before entering the promised land. Though childless and landless, he received God's promise and the circumcision covenant, fathered Isaac, and bought a Shechem tomb from Hamor's children.

l: Moses, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Moses, born in Egypt and raised by Pharaoh's daughter, is educated in Egyptian wisdom and mighty in words and works. After striking an Egyptian defending an Israelite, he is rejected and flees to Midian, fathering two sons. Forty years later God sends him as ruler and deliverer; he leads Israelites out, receives revelations at Sinai, and foretells a prophet.

l: Israelites (our fathers), The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Israelite fathers sold Joseph, went to Egypt in famine, multiplied, then suffered mistreatment. They rejected Moses, longed for Egypt, worshiped a calf and Moloch's tabernacle, yet held the testimony tabernacle into Joshua's time, and persecuted prophets, as Stephen says his hearers do.

l: healing of the lame man, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A lame man is healed when Peter, in Jesus' name, commands him to walk and takes his right hand; his feet and ankles instantly strengthen. Peter credits faith in Jesus' name, not the apostles' power. The miracle is then seen by all Jerusalem, the council cannot deny it, and everyone glorifies God.

l: repentance and restoration, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_purpose sins blotted out [result of repenting and turning again] Peter urges the people to repent and turn again so that their sins may be blotted out and times of refreshing may come from the Lord's presence. He says God may send Christ Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things spoken by the prophets, and warns through Moses that every soul that will not listen to the promised prophet will be utterly destroyed.

l: Peter and John, The Acts of the Apostles
s: are_perceived_as unlearned and ignorant men [who had been with Jesus] Peter and John are seized, held until morning, and questioned by the council. The council marvels at their boldness, perceives them as unlearned and ignorant men, and recognizes that they had been with Jesus. After being threatened and commanded not to speak in Jesus' name, they answer that they cannot help telling what they saw and heard, and they are released.

l: rulers, elders and scribes (council), The Acts of the Apostles
s: The council is the Jerusalem body of rulers, elders and scribes, including the senate of Israel, convened by the high priest. It confronts the apostles over preaching and healing in Jesus' name. First it questions Peter and John, threatens them, and releases them. Later it seeks the imprisoned apostles, resolves to kill them, yields to Gamaliel's counsel, then beats them, repeats the command, and lets them go.

l: believers, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Believers are a growing community of about five thousand men who, after Peter and John report, pray together, are filled with the Holy Spirit, speak God's word boldly, and live with one heart and soul, sharing all possessions.

l: resurrection, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The proclamation of the resurrection from the dead in Jesus is what upsets the priests, the temple captain, and the Sadducees. Peter says God raised Jesus from the dead, and the apostles give testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus with great power.

l: Gentiles, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Gentiles are non-Jewish people who come to receive God's word. In Caesarea, Cornelius's household hears Peter, receives the Holy Spirit, speaks in other languages, magnifies God, and is baptized in Jesus Christ's name. Jerusalem believers then conclude God has granted them repentance to life. Later, their turning to God brings the brothers great joy, and the council decides not to burden them with circumcision, asking only a few necessary things.

l: Barnabas, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Barnabas, also called Joses by the apostles, is a Levite from Cyprus, a good man full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and later an apostle, prophet and teacher. He begins by selling his field and laying the money at the apostles' feet. He then supports Saul, bringing him to the apostles and vouching for him when the disciples in Jerusalem feared him. Sent by the Jerusalem assembly to Antioch, he exhorts believers, fetches Saul from Tarsus, and carries relief to Judea. Set apart by the Holy Spirit with Saul (Paul), he leads the Gentile mission through Cyprus, Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, is driven out of one city, is called Jupiter by the Lystrans, and tears his clothes to stop sacrifice. They appoint elders and report back to Antioch and Jerusalem about signs and wonders among the nations. The story ends with a sharp contention with Paul over John Mark, after which Barnabas sails to Cyprus with Mark.

l: shared possessions, The Acts of the Apostles
s: None of the believers claims his possessions as his own, and they have all things in common. Owners of lands or houses sell them and lay the proceeds at the apostles' feet, so that no one lacks and distribution is made according to need.

l: prayer of the believers, The Acts of the Apostles
s: After hearing the council's threats, the believers lift their voice to God with one accord, address him as creator, and quote David's words about the nations and rulers raging against the Lord and his Christ. They apply this to Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and Israel against Jesus, and ask for boldness and for signs and wonders through Jesus' name. The place is shaken and they are all filled with the Holy Spirit.

l: interrogation of Peter and John, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The council stands Peter and John in the middle and asks by what power or name they did this. Peter answers that it was in Jesus' name, after which the council confers, commands them not to speak or teach in Jesus' name, and threatens them further. Peter and John say they must listen to God rather than the council, and they are let go.

l: Ananias, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The records gather several different figures named Ananias under one label, so it is not truly a single person. One Ananias, married to Sapphira, sold land, kept back part of the price, and laid the rest at the apostles' feet; Peter said he had lied to God, and he fell dead and was buried. Another, a disciple at Damascus, was devout according to the law and well reported of by the Jews. Told by the Lord in a vision, he went to the blinded Saul, restored his sight, and urged baptism. A third, the high priest, came with elders and Tertullus to inform the governor against Paul.

l: Sapphira, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_aware_of possession (Ananias and Sapphira's land) [knew Ananias kept back part of the price] Sapphira, aware of her husband's scheme, came in about three hours later not knowing what had happened and affirmed that the land was sold for "so much." Peter asked how they had agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord, and she fell dead at his feet. The young men buried her by her husband.

l: possession (Ananias and Sapphira's land), The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a land The land was sold by Ananias and Sapphira, who kept back part of the price and laid only a part at the apostles' feet. Peter noted that while they kept it, it remained their own, and after it was sold the price was in their power.

l: deaths of Ananias and Sapphira, The Acts of the Apostles
s: causes great fear [on the whole assembly and all who heard] Ananias fell dead after Peter's words, and about three hours later Sapphira fell dead at Peter's feet after confirming the same account. Both were carried out and buried by the young men. Great fear came on the whole assembly and on all who heard of it.

l: high priest and chief priests, The Acts of the Apostles
s: belongs_to Sadducees [the high priest and those with him are the sect of the Sadducees] The high priest, with the Sadducees, was filled with jealousy and had the apostles put in public custody. After they vanished from the prison, he was perplexed, had them brought without violence to the council, and accused them of filling Jerusalem with their teaching and intending to bring this man's blood on them. He and the council were cut to the heart and determined to kill them until Gamaliel spoke.

l: angel of the Lord, The Acts of the Apostles
s: opens public custody (prison) [by night, bringing the apostles out] An angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night and brought the apostles out. He told them to go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.

l: Gamaliel, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Gamaliel, a Pharisee and law teacher honored by all the people, sits on the council. He has the apostles briefly removed, cites Theudas and Judas as failed movements, urges leaving the apostles alone, and persuades the council.

l: beating and release of the apostles, The Acts of the Apostles
s: results_in rejoicing [counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus' name] After agreeing with Gamaliel, the council summoned the apostles, beat them, commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. The apostles departed rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus' name, and they never stopped teaching and preaching in the temple and at home.

l: Stephen, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Stephen is one of the chosen seven men, full of faith, power, and the Holy Spirit. He performs wonders and signs among the people and speaks with wisdom that opponents cannot withstand. Falsely accused of blasphemy against Moses, God, the holy place, and the law, he is seized and brought before the council, which sees his face like an angel's. He answers the high priest with a long review of Israel's history and accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit. He sees God's glory and Jesus at God's right hand, is stoned, entrusts his spirit to Jesus, asks forgiveness for his killers, and dies.

l: Hellenists, The Acts of the Apostles
s: complains_against Hebrews [over neglected widows in the daily service] The Hellenists raise a complaint against the Hebrews because their widows are neglected in the daily service.

l: Hebrews, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Hebrews are the subject of the Hellenists' complaint that the Hellenist widows are neglected in the daily service.

l: seven men, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, are chosen by the multitude to oversee the daily service: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. They are set before the apostles, who pray and lay hands on them.

l: Antioch, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Antioch is a city with Gentile believers among its residents. Hellenists there believe the preached Lord Jesus; Barnabas and Saul teach for a year, and disciples are first called Christians. It sends relief to Judea, becomes the site of the circumcision dispute and letter's reading, and Paul and Barnabas part ways.

l: synagogue disputers, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A group of synagogue men, including Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and those of Cilicia and Asia, dispute with Stephen, fail against his wisdom, then secretly induce blasphemy claims, stir the people, and seize him for the council.

l: false witnesses, The Acts of the Apostles
s: claims Jesus of Nazareth [will destroy the holy place and change Moses' customs] False witnesses are set up before the council and claim Stephen never stops speaking blasphemous words against the holy place and the law. They say they heard him declare that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs delivered by Moses.

l: council, The Acts of the Apostles
s: tries Stephen [brought before it] The council receives Stephen after he is seized and hears the false witnesses accuse him. All who sit in it fasten their eyes on him and see his face like the face of an angel.

l: law of Moses, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_read_in synagogues [every Sabbath, preached in every city from generations of old] Some believing Pharisees say Gentiles must be commanded to keep the law of Moses. James notes that Moses has long been preached in every city and read in the synagogues each Sabbath, while the council declines to impose the law on Gentile believers.

l: Joseph, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Joseph, sold into Egypt by the patriarchs out of jealousy, is delivered by God, gains Pharaoh's favor and wisdom, becomes governor of Egypt, reveals himself to his brothers on their second visit, and summons Jacob and seventy-five relatives.

l: Paul, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul, also called Saul, is a Jew born in Tarsus in Cilicia, raised in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, a Pharisee son of Pharisees, and a Roman citizen by birth. He first appears as a young man at whose feet garments were laid. He consented to Stephen's death and ravaged the assembly, dragging men and women to prison with the chief priests' authority. Near Damascus a light and the voice of Jesus stopped him; he was blinded, healed and baptized. Chosen as a vessel to bear Jesus' name before nations, kings and Israel, he proclaimed Jesus as the Christ in synagogues, escaped a plot in a basket, and was brought by Barnabas to the apostles, then sent to Tarsus. Barnabas fetched him to Antioch, where they taught for a year. The Holy Spirit separated him with Barnabas for the Gentile mission. He blinded Elymas, turned to the Gentiles after Jewish opposition, was called Mercury at Lystra, and was stoned yet rose. After a dispute over Mark he separated from Barnabas and chose Silas, strengthening assemblies in Syria and Cilicia. His journeys took him to Philippi, where he was jailed and invoked Roman status, then Thessalonica, Athens, and Corinth, where he made tents and taught a year and a half. At Ephesus he taught in the school of Tyrannus for two years, with special miracles through his hands, and planned Jerusalem and then Rome. After a riot and a plot, he passed through Macedonia and Greece, preached until midnight at Troas, and told the Ephesian elders he went bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, supporting himself by manual labor and coveting nothing. In Jerusalem he was seized in the temple, chained, and defended himself in Hebrew, asserting his citizenship. Accused by Tertullus, he was held two years under Felix at Caesarea, professing he served God according to the Way and hoped in the resurrection. He appealed to Caesar and defended himself before Agrippa. The voyage to Rome brought an angel's assurance that he must stand before Caesar. On Malta a viper bite left him unharmed, natives called him a god, and he healed Publius's father. The records end with him in Rome, guarded by a soldier, living two years in his rented house preaching God's Kingdom with all boldness and without hindrance.

l: Stephen's accusers (the council), The Acts of the Apostles
s: Stephen's accusers, the high priest and his hearers, are branded stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart and ears, resisters of the Holy Spirit, and betrayers and murderers of the Righteous One. Cut to the heart, they gnash their teeth, stop their ears, rush Stephen, and throw him out of the city.

l: stoning of Stephen, The Acts of the Apostles
s: occurs_outside city After Stephen describes his vision, the crowd throws him out of the city and stones him. The witnesses lay their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen calls on the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit, kneels, asks that the sin not be held against them, and falls asleep.

l: assembly in Jerusalem, The Acts of the Apostles
s: located_in Jerusalem The assembly in Jerusalem suffered a great persecution and was scattered throughout Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles. Its scattered members went around preaching the word.

l: Samaritans, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Samaritans listened with one accord to Philip, and men and women believed and were baptized. They received the Holy Spirit when Peter and John prayed and laid hands on them, and Peter and John later preached the Good News in many Samaritan villages. Earlier they had listened to Simon the sorcerer and called him the great power of God.

l: Simon, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Simon is a long-practicing sorcerer in Samaria, called the great power of God, who amazed the people. He believed, was baptized, and followed Philip, then offered the apostles money for the power to give the Holy Spirit. Peter rebuked him as bitter and in iniquity's bondage; Simon asked for prayer.

l: Ethiopian eunuch, The Acts of the Apostles
s: An Ethiopian man of great authority under Queen Candace, overseeing all her treasure. Returning from worship in Jerusalem, he reads Isaiah in his chariot, asks Philip to explain it, hears about Jesus, is baptized, and departs rejoicing.

l: Isaiah passage, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_from Isaiah [prophet] The eunuch was reading a passage from Isaiah about one led like a sheep to slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, whose judgment was taken away and whose life is taken from the earth. The eunuch asked whether the prophet meant himself or someone else, and Philip, beginning from this Scripture, preached Jesus to him.

l: Caesarea, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Caesarea is where Paul is kept in custody and where Festus returns after his stay in Jerusalem. Festus sits on the judgment seat there to hear Paul. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive there, and Paul is brought before Agrippa and the others there.

l: Aeneas, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Aeneas, a Lydda man bedridden eight years with paralysis, is told by Peter that Jesus Christ heals him; he rises immediately, prompting everyone in Lydda and Sharon to turn to the Lord.

l: Tabitha, The Acts of the Apostles
