s: Tabitha, also called Dorcas, was a disciple at Joppa known for good works and mercy, shown by garments she made for widows; she fell sick and died, then Peter raised her alive.

l: Damascus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Damascus is a city with synagogues, the destination of Saul/Paul's journey to arrest believers. On the road a great light and Jesus' voice stop him; he enters blind, is healed by Ananias, baptized, and preaches Christ. Plotting Jews watch the gates; he escapes over the wall in a basket.

l: Lydda, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Lydda was where Peter visited the saints and healed the paralyzed Aeneas. Its inhabitants, along with those of Sharon, turned to the Lord after seeing him. It was near Joppa, from which disciples sent for Peter.

l: Joppa, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Joppa is a seaside place near Lydda where Tabitha died and Peter raised her; the event spread widely, many believed, and Peter stayed with Simon the tanner.

l: Jews, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Jews appear as a recurring body opposing Paul across his ministry. At Damascus, confounded by his proof that Jesus is the Christ, they plot to kill him, and he escapes. At Corinth they blaspheme, prompting him to turn to the Gentiles, and they bring him before Gallio, who dismisses them. Many thousands of Jews have believed and are zealous for the law, yet rumors say Paul teaches forsaking Moses; Asian Jews stir a crowd in the temple to kill him. Paul identifies himself as a Jew, born in Tarsus and zealous for God. They later join Tertullus's accusations before Felix, who, seeking their favor, leaves Paul in bonds.

l: Paul's vision on the road to Damascus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul's heavenly vision on the road to Damascus was a noon encounter in which a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shone around Saul and his companions. He fell to the earth and heard Jesus ask why he persecuted him, while companions heard the sound but saw no one. Left blind, he was led into Damascus to learn what to do. The vision commissioned him as servant and witness to all, including Gentiles, and Paul says he was obedient to it.

l: Saul's blindness and healing, The Acts of the Apostles
s: lasts three days [without sight, neither ate nor drank] Saul rose from the ground unable to see, was led by hand into Damascus, and went three days without sight, food or drink. Ananias laid hands on him, something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received sight, rose, and was baptized.

l: Tabitha's resurrection, The Acts of the Apostles
s: results_in belief in the Lord [throughout Joppa] After Tabitha died and was laid in an upper room, Peter was sent for and found the widows weeping. He sent everyone out, knelt and prayed, told her to get up, and presented her alive; many in Joppa believed in the Lord.

l: Cornelius, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Cornelius is a centurion of the Italian Regiment living in Caesarea, devout and God-fearing with his whole household, generous to the needy, constantly prayerful, and well spoken of by the Jewish nation. After an angel's vision he sends men to Joppa for Peter, gathers relatives and friends, and tries to worship Peter, who refuses. He and his household hear Peter's message, receive the Holy Spirit, and are baptized. Peter later retells the angel's report.

l: angel (sent to Cornelius), The Acts of the Apostles
s: An angel of God appears to Cornelius at about the ninth hour and says his prayers and gifts to the needy have gone up as a memorial before God. He tells Cornelius to send men to Joppa to get Simon, who is also called Peter, and says where he is staying, with a tanner named Simon by the sea. Cornelius later describes him as a man in bright clothing, and the visitors call him a holy angel.

l: vision of the sheet (Peter's vision), The Acts of the Apostles
s: While Peter prays on the housetop around noon, he sees heaven opened and a great sheet let down by four corners, holding all kinds of four-footed animals, wild animals, reptiles, and birds. A voice tells him to rise, kill and eat, and says that what God has cleansed he must not call unclean. This happens three times before the sheet is taken up into heaven, and Peter is perplexed until Cornelius's men arrive; he later applies it to people, saying he should call no man unholy or unclean. In a trance at Joppa, Peter saw a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners, containing four-footed animals, wild animals, creeping things, and birds. A voice told him to kill and eat, and after he refused, said not to call unclean what God has cleansed. This happened three times before everything was drawn back up to heaven.

l: clean and unclean (dietary and social), The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_determined_by God [what God has cleansed must not be called unclean] Peter declares in the vision that he has never eaten anything common or unclean, but the voice answers that what God has cleansed he must not call unclean. Peter explains in Caesarea that it is unlawful for a Jew to join himself to or visit one of another nation, but that God has shown him he should call no man unholy or unclean. The distinction is thus extended from foods to people.

l: Peter's sermon, The Acts of the Apostles
s: In Cornelius's house Peter opens by saying God shows no favoritism and accepts in every nation the one who fears him and works righteousness. He recounts the gospel of Jesus: his anointing, ministry of doing good and healing, death on a tree, resurrection on the third day, appearance to chosen witnesses, and appointment as Judge. He closes by saying all the prophets testify that everyone who believes in Jesus's name will receive remission of sins, and the Holy Spirit falls on the hearers while he is still speaking.

l: those of the circumcision, The Acts of the Apostles
s: contended_with Peter [over eating with uncircumcised men] Those of the circumcision contend with Peter in Jerusalem, objecting that he went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them. After hearing his account, they hold their peace and glorify God.

l: scattered believers, The Acts of the Apostles
s: scattered_by oppression about Stephen Those scattered by the oppression that arose about Stephen travel to Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, at first speaking only to Jews. Some men of Cyprus and Cyrene then preach the Lord Jesus to the Hellenists in Antioch, and a great number believe.

l: Agabus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Agabus is a prophet from Judea who comes to Caesarea, binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt, and prophesies in the Holy Spirit's name that Jews in Jerusalem will bind and deliver its owner to Gentiles.

l: famine, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A worldwide famine, foretold by the prophet Agabus by the Spirit at Antioch, which then occurs during the reign of Claudius.

l: relief for the brothers in Judea, The Acts of the Apostles
s: sent_to elders [by Barnabas and Saul] Each Antioch disciple, according to their means, determines to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. They do so, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

l: King Herod, The Acts of the Apostles
s: King Herod oppresses the assembly, kills James the brother of John with the sword, and arrests Peter, but Peter escapes and Herod has the guards executed. He goes to Caesarea, angry with Tyre and Sidon, gives a speech in royal clothing, accepts the crowd's cry that he is a god, and an angel strikes him; worms eat him and he dies.

l: angel of the Lord, The Acts of the Apostles
s: An angel of the Lord appears in Peter's cell with a light, strikes Peter on the side to wake him, and tells him to get dressed, put on his sandals and cloak, and follow. He leads Peter past the first and second guard to the iron gate, which opens by itself, and departs after they go down one street. Later an angel of the Lord strikes Herod because he did not give God the glory.

l: prison (where Peter was held), The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_part iron gate [leads into the city] The prison is where Herod puts Peter under guard of four squads of four soldiers, with guards in front of the door. Peter is bound with two chains in the cell between two soldiers. He leaves it with the angel, passing the first and second guard and an iron gate that opens by itself, and the next morning the soldiers are in a stir over what became of him.

l: Rhoda, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a servant girl [at the house of Mary] Rhoda is a servant girl who comes to answer when Peter knocks at the door of the gate at Mary's house. She recognizes his voice and, for joy, runs in to report that he is standing there without opening the gate. When told she is crazy, she insists it is so.

l: the Lord, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Lord is credited with sending out his angel and delivering Peter from the hand of Herod and from everything the Jewish people were expecting. Peter declares how the Lord brought him out of the prison. His angel strikes Herod, and the word of God grows and multiplies.

l: Antioch of Pisidia, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_part synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia Paul and Barnabas arrive here from Perga and enter the synagogue on the Sabbath, where Paul preaches. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers to hear the word, but Jewish opposition and a persecution stirred up among prominent women and men lead to the missionaries' expulsion.

l: Elymas, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Elymas, also called Bar Jesus, is a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet with proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos. He opposes Barnabas and Saul, seeking to turn the proconsul from the faith, and is struck blind for a season.

l: Sergius Paulus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Sergius Paulus, discerning proconsul at Paphos, summons Barnabas and Saul to hear God's word, then believes in Jesus, astonished, after seeing Elymas struck blind.

l: Jews of Antioch of Pisidia, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Jews of Antioch of Pisidia are a group who, after some follow Paul and Barnabas, grow jealous when crowds gather, contradict and blaspheme Paul, then incite prominent women and chief men to persecute and expel the missionaries.

l: Gentiles, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Gentiles at Antioch ask to hear the message again, nearly the whole city gathers, Paul and Barnabas turn to them, and they rejoice, glorify God's word, and those appointed to eternal life believe and spread it.

l: Iconium, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Iconium is a city with a Jewish synagogue where Paul and Barnabas preached; many believed, but the city split between Jews and apostles, a stoning plot forced their flight, Iconium Jews later incited Lystra, and the apostles returned to strengthen disciples.

l: Paul's sermon at Antioch of Pisidia, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul's synagogue sermon at Antioch of Pisidia, after the law and prophets are read, surveys Israel's history from exodus to David, proclaims Jesus' death and resurrection, offers forgiveness beyond Moses' law, and warns scoffers.

l: salvation and forgiveness through Jesus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Salvation through Jesus: Paul proclaims remission of sins and justification for everyone who believes, beyond what Moses' law could achieve. The message goes first to Israel's children and God-fearers, then to the Gentiles as light to earth's ends.

l: Gentile mission, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_commanded_by God [light for the Gentiles to bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth] After the Holy Spirit sends out Barnabas and Saul, they proclaim the word first in synagogues, but at Antioch of Pisidia they declare that, since the Jews reject it, they turn to the Gentiles. They cite the Lord's command that they be a light for the Gentiles bringing salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.

l: Lystra, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Lystra is a Lycaonian-speaking city in Lycaonia where apostles flee, heal a lame man, are mistaken for gods, Paul is stoned, and later they return to strengthen disciples.

l: Jews (opponents of Paul and Barnabas), The Acts of the Apostles
s: Unbelieving Jews in Iconium stir up the Gentiles against the brothers and join in a plot to mistreat and stone the apostles. Jews from Antioch and Iconium then come to Lystra, persuade the crowds, and stone Paul, dragging him out of the city.

l: crowd of Lystra (multitude at Lystra), The Acts of the Apostles
s: After seeing the healing, the crowd cries out in the Lycaonian language that the gods have come down in the likeness of men. They call Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury, and with their priest they nearly sacrifice to them, being hardly restrained. Persuaded by Jews from Antioch and Iconium, they then join in stoning Paul.

l: lame man (man at Lystra), The Acts of the Apostles
s: A man at Lystra, crippled in his feet from his mother's womb and never having walked, listens to Paul speak. Paul sees that he has faith to be made whole and tells him to stand upright, and he leaps up and walks.

l: healing of the lame man, The Acts of the Apostles
s: performed_by Paul [at Lystra] Paul, seeing the man's faith, commands him with a loud voice to stand upright, and the man leaps up and walks. The miracle leads the Lystra crowd to take the apostles for gods and attempt a sacrifice to them.

l: stoning of Paul, The Acts of the Apostles
s: occurred_in Lystra [Paul dragged out of the city] Jews from Antioch and Iconium persuade the Lystra crowds, who stone Paul and drag him out of the city, supposing him dead. As disciples stand around him, he rises, re-enters the city, and the next day leaves with Barnabas for Derbe.

l: Good News, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The apostles preach the Good News in Lystra and Derbe after fleeing Iconium, and make many disciples in Derbe. Paul tells the Lystrans that the Good News calls them to turn from vain things to the living God.

l: Silas, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Silas is a prophet and a chief man among the brothers, also a Roman citizen. Chosen with Judas Barsabbas to carry the letter to Antioch and confirm it by word, he encourages the brothers, then Paul takes him as companion. In Philippi he is beaten, imprisoned in stocks, and prays and sings with Paul at midnight. He then joins Paul in Thessalonica, is sent to Beroea, stays there with Timothy, and is summoned to Athens.

l: Pharisees, The Acts of the Apostles
s: confesses resurrection of the dead [also confess angel and spirit] The Pharisees confess the resurrection, angels, and spirits, and Paul identifies himself as a Pharisee and son of Pharisees. Some of their scribes contend they find no evil in Paul and suggest that a spirit or angel may have spoken to him, urging that they not fight against God.

l: men from Judea, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Men from Judea came down teaching brothers that circumcision after Moses' custom was required for salvation; the Jerusalem letter says they lacked apostolic commandment and troubled and unsettled Gentile believers' souls.

l: apostles and elders, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The apostles and elders receive Paul and Barnabas in Jerusalem and gather to examine the matter. They, with the whole assembly, choose men to send to Antioch and write the letter, stating it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to lay no greater burden.

l: circumcision requirement, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a yoke [Peter's view; neither fathers nor apostles could bear it] The claim that circumcision after Moses' custom is necessary for salvation is taught by the men from Judea and urged by believing Pharisees. It is rejected in the council's outcome, which lays no such burden on Gentile believers.

l: Jerusalem council, The Acts of the Apostles
s: decides no greater burden on Gentiles than necessary things [seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them] The apostles and elders gather after much discussion, hearing Peter, Barnabas and Paul, and James. They reach one accord that Gentile believers should not be burdened beyond a few necessary things and decide to send a letter.

l: letter to Gentile believers, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A letter from the apostles, elders, and brothers to Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, disowning those who troubled them and stating necessary things; carried by Judas, Silas, Paul, Barnabas, and read in Antioch, prompting rejoicing.

l: necessary things (Gentile requirements), The Acts of the Apostles
s: Gentile believers are required to abstain from food offered to idols, blood, strangled things, and sexual immorality; the Chapter 15 letter concludes that keeping from these will bring them well-being.

l: Timothy, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Timothy is a disciple at Lystra, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. Paul wants him to accompany him and circumcises him because of the Jews who knew his father was Greek.

l: Lydia, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Lydia, a God-worshiping seller of purple from Thyatira, has her heart opened by the Lord to Paul's words at the riverside, is baptized with her household, then hosts the company and later meets the brothers.

l: jailer, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A jailer guards Paul and Silas in stocks, nearly kills himself after an earthquake opens the doors, is stopped by Paul, asks how to be saved, hears the word, tends their wounds, is baptized with his household, and rejoices believing God.

l: girl with a spirit of divination, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A girl with a divination spirit earns her masters much gain by fortune telling. She follows Paul and others for many days, proclaiming them servants of the Most High God, until Paul commands the spirit out in Jesus Christ's name.

l: girl's masters, The Acts of the Apostles
s: When the spirit is gone, the masters see that the hope of their gain is lost and seize Paul and Silas. They drag them before the rulers and accuse them of agitating the city as Jews and advocating customs unlawful for Romans.

l: magistrates, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The magistrates tear the clothes from Paul and Silas and order them beaten with rods and jailed. The next day they send sergeants to release them, but they become afraid on learning the two are Romans, and they come, beg them, bring them out, and ask them to leave the city.

l: Macedonia, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Macedonia is the region from which a man in Paul's night vision begs him to come over and help. Concluding the Lord has called them to preach the Good News there, the company sails to Neapolis and on to Philippi.

l: Philippi, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Philippi is a Roman colony and foremost city of Macedonia, where the company stays; Lydia's household is baptized, a girl is freed of her spirit, and Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned.

l: prison, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_part inner prison [where Paul and Silas were held in stocks] The prison holds Paul and Silas in its inner part with their feet in stocks, while other prisoners listen to their hymns. At midnight its foundations shake and its doors open, and afterward Paul and Silas leave it and go to Lydia's house.

l: earthquake, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_effect opened prison doors [also loosened everyone's bonds] A great earthquake strikes about midnight while Paul and Silas pray and sing, shaking the prison's foundations. All the doors open and everyone's bonds are loosened, which leads the jailer to draw his sword and then to ask how to be saved.

l: beating of Paul and Silas, The Acts of the Apostles
s: ordered_by magistrates [beaten with rods] The magistrates, with the multitude rising against them, have Paul and Silas's clothes torn off and order them beaten with rods, laying many stripes on them before the prison. Paul later protests that it was done publicly and without a trial to men who are Romans, which frightens the magistrates.

l: Thessalonica, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_place_of_worship synagogue (Thessalonica) [Jewish synagogue] Thessalonica had a Jewish synagogue where Paul reasoned for three Sabbaths; some Jews, a great multitude of devout Greeks and many chief women joined him. Unpersuaded Jews raised a mob and brought Jason and other brothers before the city rulers, who were troubled and took security from them. The Beroeans are described as more noble than those in Thessalonica.

l: Beroea, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul and Silas were sent there by night and went into the Jewish synagogue. The people received the word with readiness and examined the Scriptures daily, and many Jews, prominent Greek women and not a few men believed. Jews from Thessalonica came and agitated the crowds, so Paul was sent away.
